card.sound: A nervous, spitting bass made to sit under a vocal. A pair of fat saws, stacked and held steady, push through a resonant filter that snaps at the start of every note, and the whole thing is driven hard enough to be gritty and warm without getting piercing. It is nearly dry: a quick slap and a small spring sit behind each note as an afterthought, lifting it a little, and never getting anywhere near as loud as the note itself.
card.gear:
• Korg MS-20 — the resonant filter and its bite: nasty, biting, resonant.
  • Minimoog — the stacked saws: fat, thick.
  • Roland SH-101 — the tight snap at the front of a note: tight, punchy.
  • ProCo RAT — the driven edge: gritty, crunchy.

Closest to: an MS-20 bass through a RAT.
card.play:
• Register: low. It was voiced on a riff from A1 (55 Hz) up to A2 and on sixteenth-note bursts of A1, C2, D2 and E2; other registers are untested. About half of the energy on the low riff sits under 60 Hz, which is the A1 fundamental itself: it is the 100 Hz and up that carries it on a small speaker, and whether it is heard enough under a vocal on a PA is for the room.
  • Touch and gate: short, detached notes are its home (80 to 150 ms gates were measured). The filter snap gives the "spit": on an isolated A1 the first 23 ms are about 1.8 times as bright (centroid) as the next 67 ms.
  • It is MONO, so legato does not re-fire the envelopes: a key still held when the next one goes down slides to the new note without a new snap. Play it detached for the spit. A chord plays one note (the last).
  • Stable on purpose: the pitch wander measured 0.3 cents (s.d., the engine's log of the voice, held A2) on this variant, C, with VINTAGE 10, no LFO, no glide.
  • The wet is small, and it is measured. Behind a note the slap and spring return is, in the loudest of three isolated notes, 43.6 dB under the dry note in the first 20 ms, 25.0 dB under at 20 to 100 ms and 16.5 dB under at 100 to 250 ms (that last window is the tightest, since a 150 ms note is already ending in it). After the key goes up the level is 20 dB down at 24 ms, 40 dB down at 214 ms and 60 dB down at 436 ms; the voice alone is 60 dB down at 54 ms. So there is a short wet tail of about half a second.
  • Costs, honestly: the grit comes partly from a GROWL step, which costs about +595 host instr/sample whenever it is on; the worst case for the patch is about 1640 host instr/sample (the original: 317). The device build was not run; the render time on the device is not measured.
  • Slot 1 is the boot patch. Changing it shifts the first moments of echo and spring programs loaded straight after power-on by a small amount (the filter smoothing carries the boot patch's state); see the voicing README, section 12.
  • Tricks: untested on this patch: the SLOBBER slop ride (it will loosen the deliberately steady pair), SEQ held (Tape Stop), the kill switch (HEEL), CHEW. More GROWL than 46 or more echo than the measured amount is untested for the "never above the note" rule; a variant with the wet turned up was rendered, and there the echo came to about 6 dB under the note in the last window.
  • Level: matched to the bank reference on the low riff (-18.0 dBFS RMS; peak -12.8 on the whole render; phrase (b) reads -18.0 too).

card.sound: A low-mid grinder built from a pair of fat pulse waves whose widths sweep quickly, so every note shudders and churns on purpose: a clear, fast pulse-width wobble you can hear on the riff, not a shimmer. The filter bites, it is pushed into a moderate crunch, and each note starts with a little skid and a snap. It is thick and dry, and it hits hard.
card.gear:
• Roland Juno-60 — the pulse-width movement: PWM, wobble, thick.
  • Korg Polysix — the stacked pulses: fat, PWM.
  • Roland SH-101 — the punchy PWM bass: PWM bass, punchy.
  • ProCo RAT — the crunch: crunchy.
  • Korg MS-20 — the filter: biting.

Closest to: a Juno-60 PWM bass through a RAT.
card.play:
• Register and gate: it was voiced on a riff of A2 (110 Hz) up to E3 with G2, in notes of about 400 ms (long enough for the PWM to swing two or three times inside each note) and on a held A2, plus a few 150 ms chops. Other registers are untested.
  • The PWM, measured: the sweep runs at about 11.5 Hz. On a held A2 it moves the 150 to 400 Hz band by 11.9 dB from the top of its swing to the bottom, the 400 to 1,200 Hz band by 6.7 dB, the 1.2 to 3 kHz band by 5.3 dB and the 3 kHz and up band by 5.4 dB, and the overall level by 4.1 dB; on the riff's 400 ms notes the same band moves 8.0 dB and the level 2.9 dB. Each detached note restarts the sweep from the same place.
  • One LFO does both jobs. The pulse-width sweep and the filter wobble share the single LFO and run at the same rate; the slow half-hertz filter wobble the original patch had is gone. There is no way to slow one without the other.
  • A PWM sweep that crosses 50 % doubles its rate (a pulse and its mirror width sound alike). Here the widths run from about 18 to 55 %, so it crosses 50 % by a few points at the top of each swing; the measured rate still matches the LFO's, so it is not doubling. Do not push the PWM depth much further.
  • It is MONO, so legato does not re-fire the envelopes: a key held while the next goes down glides to it (the GLIDE is set for the skid) without a new snap. Play it detached. A chord plays one note.
  • Thickness: the two pulses sit about 8 cents apart (a beat of about half a hertz at A2); the sound is dense and heavily driven, and its peak-to-RMS ratio is 3.2 dB.
  • Costs, honestly: about 298 host instr/sample in the worst case (the original: 309); no GROWL. The device build was not run.
  • Tricks: untested on this patch: the SLOBBER slop ride, SEQ held (Tape Stop), the kill switch (HEEL), GROWL, any effect. Two other versions were rendered, one at 7.7 Hz without the filter wobble and a slower, deeper one with a wider pair; nothing else was tried.
  • Level: matched to the bank reference on the grind riff (-17.9 dBFS RMS, peak -14.6; phrase (b) reads -18.0, where a chord plays only its last note). The sound stops at once: 60 dB down 26 ms after the key goes up.

card.sound: Fat, slop-heavy dual saws with a sub-octave underneath: seasick, never quite in tune with itself, and thick without going murky. Short notes are chopped stone-dead by the gate, and the tail doesn't fade, it sputters — a few ragged stutters as the note dies. It is a raw, dry, engine-only sound with no effects on it: the drift and the chop are the whole point. This is the DØG-5 thesis in a single patch.
card.gear:
• Korg Mono/Poly — detuned oscillators that drift and never settle: fat, slop, seasick, thick.
  • Sequential Prophet-5 (early, tuning-unstable revisions) — the dual-saw warmth with the drift: fat, warm, drift.
  • Minimoog — the body under the instability: fat, sub-heavy, thick.
  • Korg MS-20 — the bite and the spit in the filter and the tail: nasty, biting, spitting.

Closest to: Korg Mono/Poly — its drifting, detuned saw chaos, with Minimoog weight underneath, chopped by the gate.
card.play:
• Register: low to low-mid. Roots and fifths from about A1 to A3 are where the sub and the pair sit best. Fifth-and-octave power chords are its home ground.
  • Touch and gate: play it staccato. Short notes, roughly 150–180 ms, are where it works as intended: a clean, hard body and a sputtering tail.
  • Where it does not work: the sputter is tied to how long the note has been sounding, not to the key coming up. A note held past about a fifth of a second spits all the way through, and very short notes (under about 100 ms) only catch the start of it. Long held pads and sustained leads are the wrong job; use it for riffs and stabs.
  • Chords: polyphony is set to POLY 6 because every note is two voices. Two- and three-note chords (a fifth, or a fifth with the octave) play in full. A fourth note in a chord, or a very busy run, steals voices from the notes before it: keep chords to three notes.
  • Tricks that suit it:
  • ALGORITHM slop ride (SLOBBER): the best one. The patch already drifts; the ride pushes it from seasick to dying-tape-motor, at up to about 3.8 times the patch's own slop. At full ride a single held note sits about 20 cents flat and a chord about 3 cents flat (accepted character).
  • Tape Stop (SEQ held) on the riff as an ending; it dives the whole sound.
  • Kill switch (HEEL) for a dead stop mid-riff: the sound and the sputter stop at once.
  • Macros (GROWL, ALLEY, DRAIN, CHEW): all at 0 on purpose. Untested on this patch, so treat them as open: the dry chop is the sound, and a wash of ALLEY or DRAIN on the tail will bury the sputter.

card.sound: A tearing hard-sync lead: the pitch of the synced oscillator rips down on every note, nasal and biting, with a plain saw underneath for body. A pair of voices detuned slightly apart makes it fat enough to cut through a drum machine, and the note stops dead when you let go, with only a faint quick slap behind it. It is raw on purpose: that is where the rip lives.
card.gear:
• Sequential Pro-One — the sync sweep itself: sync, punchy, ripping.
  • Sequential Prophet-5 — the fatness of a doubled voice: sync, fat.
  • ARP Odyssey — the nasal, cutting tone: nasal, biting.
  • Moog Prodigy — the cheap, raw edge: fat, cheap, raw.

Closest to: a Pro-One sync lead.
card.play:
• Register: mid, roughly A3 to A4 and around it, where the lead was auditioned. It is a one-note-at-a-time lead: no chords.
  • Touch and gate: play it staccato. The rip comes from the filter envelope sweeping the synced oscillator, and in MONO and UNISON a note struck while another is still held slides in and does not re-fire the envelopes. So the sweep fires on detached notes only; a legato run glides (a short slide is set) but rips just once, on its first note.
  • The stop: the voice itself stops dead on release. The echo is not gated, so a faint slap follows each note; it is quiet and short (a 1/16 slap), and turning the echo's MIX down to 0 gives a literal dead stop.
  • Tricks that suit it:
  • ALGORITHM slop ride (SLOBBER): pulls the two voices apart; untested on this patch.
  • Kill switch (HEEL) for an instant stop, including the slap. Untested on this patch.
  • Tape Stop (SEQ held) on a held note as a dive. Untested on this patch.
  • GROWL (adding it live): more edge on top of the filter DRIVE the patch already has; untested here, and GROWL below about 28 does little.
  • DRAIN: at 0 on purpose (no spring); a wash will blur the rip.
  • Level: it is set to the bank's level on its lead phrase. Its own volume is a little below the default (about 1.6 dB), because the two-voice stack is louder than the one-voice version (which needed about 3 dB more).

card.sound:
A kick substitute made of a single square wave. The pitch drops fast at the very start, and a fast random stepped pitch LFO moves it to a new random value again and again, so each hit gets a few random pitch steps (a longer note gets more). The wave stays almost entirely at its extreme levels, there is no attack, and the hit stops quickly when you let go. It is dry: no tape, no drive stage, no echo, no spring.

The owner's own description of the intent: pixelated, gritty, blown out, like a photocopy reduced to pure black and white. That is the intent, not a measurement.
card.gear:
• Roland TR-808 kick — sub, thump.
  • Roland SH-101 — sub, thick.
  • Tascam Portastudio cassette 4-track — lo-fi, noisy.
  • ProCo RAT — crunchy, driven.

Closest to: an 808 kick smashed onto a blown-out cassette 4-track.

Nothing here says the patch matches these: it was built from the descriptions, by measurement, and approved by ear. The tape part of that picture is not in this patch: the tape was removed in round 2 at the owner's direction (CHEW, HISS and DROPS are 0), and the drive stage (GROWL) is not used either.
card.play:
• Register: it was voiced on three isolated 150 ms hits (A0 27.5 Hz, A1 55 Hz, A2 110 Hz) and four hits a bar of A1 at 120 BPM; the pilot riff and stabs phrases were rendered too. Other registers are untested.
  • It is MONO, so legato does not re-fire the envelopes: a key held while the next goes down slides to the new note and the envelopes do not restart. Play it detached. A chord plays one note (the last).
  • What is in the voice: one hard square (OSC 2 pulse, an octave up from the key, OSC 1 off), the filter open (12 dB, CUTOFF 105, RESO 0), amp and filter attack 0, a decay of 187 ms to sustain 0, a 2 ms release. The quick pitch drop is the filter envelope on OSC 2's pitch: +17 semitones at the strike, falling over 11 ms.
  • The glitch: the LFO is sample-and-hold on pitch, 21 Hz, depth up to ±4.7 semitones (±470 cents), free-running. The hit-to-hit spread of the first-60-ms centroid over eight pattern hits (s.d. over mean) is 5 % with the LFO as shipped (LFO PITCH 80), 1 % with the LFO off (LFO PITCH 0) and 10 % at LFO PITCH 110. The ratio of 150–400 Hz energy to 1.2 kHz+ energy (A1, 20–100 ms) is 3.9 as shipped (PITCH 80) and 26.5 at PITCH 110. Other LFO rates are untested.
  • Black and white, measured: the share of samples within 10 % of the rail (5 ms windows, first 100 ms of a hit) is 98 / 96 / 94 % on A0 / A1 / A2 (a decaying hard-clipped square reads near 100 %). Above 1.2 kHz is 0.9 / 3.4 / 5.6 % of the energy in the first 100 ms.
  • Tail: 60 dB down 16 ms after the key goes up on A1 and A2, and 8 ms on A0 (DC subtracted). A1 falls from −12 to −29 dBFS (20 ms windows) over its first 120 ms.
  • The kick is mostly the quick pitch drop. There is no click spike in the patch: the first 5 ms measure 3.1 dB over the 10–50 ms level, which is in step with the decay. A filter-envelope click was tried (CUTOFF 85, ENV AMT 100–127, DECAY 25–30): it closed the filter, leaving 1.3 % of the energy above 1.2 kHz against 3.4 % and 85–89 % black-and-white against 96 %, so it is not in the patch.
  • A0 is still mostly sub: after its first 20 ms, 81 % of the A0 energy is under 60 Hz, and a 27.5 Hz square is inaudible on a small speaker. In its first 20 ms 45 % is at 60–150 Hz. A1 and A2 sit above that: after a 100 Hz high-pass the kick phrase keeps −1.6 dB of its level (the original: −10.9).
  • Level: −18.1 dBFS RMS on the kick phrase (11 hits × 150 ms), phrase (b) −19.1, peak −10.7 dBFS; crest factor 7.3 dB over the kick phrase and 1.9 dB over the first 30 ms of a hit. VOLUME is 123 of 127: there is almost no knob headroom above the bank reference. A tighter decay (DECAY 72) already reads −19.5 dBFS at VOLUME 123.
  • Not bit-comparable from the boot patch: the sample-and-hold LFO follows the engine's random state, and the audio differs between the boot patch and INIT (the difference between the two renders is 1.9 to 2.9 dB louder than the signal on the test phrases; they are bit-identical when both load from INIT). The cause was not isolated.
  • Costs, honestly: about 1337 host instr/sample worst case (idle 1164, the engine alone, plus 173 under load; the original 1361). Not used here: GROWL 104 would add about 595 and CHEW 127 about 784 (measured on the round-2 test patch). The device build was not run and the render time on the device is not measured.
  • Tricks: untested on this patch: the SLOBBER slop ride, SEQ held (Tape Stop), the kill switch (HEEL), ALLEY, DRAIN, GROWL, CHEW.

card.sound: The fuzz weapon: a huge, thick wall. A pair of fat saws on every voice are pushed hard into the drive until the sound is flat and relentless, and it simply does not die while you hold the key. The strike is quick and snappy, the filter and its resonance are wide open, and when you let go there is a short tail rather than a ring. It is completely dry: no echo, no spring, nothing springy or boingy. A power chord stays whole.
card.gear:
• Death by Audio Fuzz War — the benchmark, a huge fuzz beast: fuzzy, thick wall.
  • Electro-Harmonix Big Muff — the wall: fuzzy, thick wall.
  • Fuzz Face — the fuzz: fuzzy, spitting.
  • Univox Super-Fuzz — voltage-starved, spitting.
  • Korg Mono/Poly — as the source: fat, drifting.
  • Realistic Concertmate MG-1 — voltage-starved, lo-fi.

Closest to: a Mono/Poly into a Big Muff.

Nothing here says the patch matches the benchmark: it was built toward it from the descriptions, by measurement, and approved by ear. The "voltage-starved" gating and sputter of the Super-Fuzz and the MG-1 is not claimed: nothing in this patch gates (BIAS only raises the peaks).
card.play:
• Register and touch: it was voiced on a held A2 (3 s), a held power chord (A2, E3, A3, 1.5 s), 300 ms power-chord stabs and a low A1. Other registers are untested.
  • The wall, measured: the held note's peak-to-RMS ratio is 1.7 dB (a square wave is 0, a sine 3), and the level over a 3 s hold falls by 0.0 dB, first half second to last. The held power chord is at 3.2 dB. The source is POLY with 6 voices, so a three-note chord plays whole; the number of notes it keeps before stealing is the 6 voices.
  • The strike: AMP ATTACK is 2.4 ms in the engine's time table; measured on a high probe note, the voice alone rises from 10 to 90 % in 2.0 ms (and the fuzzed note in 1.0 ms), with the level -0.3 dB at 2 ms against its plateau when struck from silence. It is not a zero attack. The strike is only +0.3 dB over the plateau: the fuzz flattens the dynamics, so the "punch" is in the quick rise, not in a level spike; more punch means less GROWL.
  • The tail: 60 dB down 278 ms after a 3 s note and 314 ms after the held chord.
  • The filter: wide open, with RESO 80. The filter does not sing by itself until about RESO 124 on this patch (measured on this variant, C, with the probe re-run: the noise-fed filter answers a 12 dB drop in its input with 12.0 dB at RESO 100 and 115, 11.8 at 120, 3.3 at 124 and 0.3 at 127; 12 = linear, far less = singing), so there is room above 80 but not above about 120.
  • Reads about 2 dB hot on phrase (b): it was matched to the bank reference (-18.1 dBFS RMS) on its own wall phrase of held notes and chords; on phrase (b) it reads -16.1 dBFS, about 2 dB hotter. The cause of that difference was not isolated. The signal is heavily compressed (RMS and peak sit 5 dB apart on the wall phrase). VOLUME is the lever.
  • VOLUME changes how a note from silence starts. GROWL's loudness trim reads the output stage, so the level of the first moments depends on VOLUME; set VOLUME first, then judge the strike.
  • It is POLY, not MONO or UNISON, so every key re-fires the envelopes. Legato does not matter here.
  • Costs, honestly: the GROWL at 104 costs about +595 host instr/sample whenever it is on; the worst case for the patch is about 1414 host instr/sample (the original: 317). The device build was not run; the render time on the device is not measured.
  • Tricks: untested on this patch: the SLOBBER slop ride, SEQ held (Tape Stop), the kill switch (HEEL), CHEW, ALLEY and DRAIN (all at 0 on purpose: dry is the brief). A version with a lower GROWL and one with four saws a note (DUAL) were rendered; the DUAL costs about 1964 host instr/sample.

card.sound: A fat square with a wobble in its pitch, chopped short. A pair of square waves a hair apart, one frequency-modulating the other so the tone carries extra energy below the note, and a random pitch wobble. Notes stop quickly when you let go, and a tape stage on the end delays every note slightly. It is dry: no echo, no spring.
card.gear:
• Korg Mono/Poly — the source: fat, drifting.
  • Sequential Prophet-5 — wobble, nervous.
  • Roland RE-201 Space Echo — the tape stage: wobble, lo-fi.
  • Roland SH-101 — punchy.

Closest to: a Mono/Poly cross-mod square through a worn tape echo.

Nothing here says the patch matches these: it was built toward the descriptions, by measurement, and approved by ear.
card.play:
• Register: it was voiced on a held A2 (2.4 s), twelve 60 ms staccato notes from A2 up to G3, and three 80 ms A3 notes; other registers are untested.
  • It is MONO, so legato does not re-fire the envelopes: a key held while the next goes down slides to the new note and the envelopes do not restart. Play it detached. A chord plays one note (the last).
  • Where the wobble comes from: the random pitch LFO (5.7 Hz, a new target about every 176 ms, up to ±19 cents). Measured on the held A2 the pitch track has a standard deviation of 9.6 cents (28 cents from 5th to 95th percentile); without the tape (CHEW 0) it is 8.9.
  • What X-MOD does: it adds sidebands and energy below the note, and it does not move the measured pitch. On the held A2 the share of energy under 60 Hz is 2 % at X-MOD 70 (0 % at 0 and 40, 10 % at 100, 18 % at 127); the cause of that low-end energy was not isolated (it suggests FM sidebands). The pitch track's spread showed no order across X-MOD 0 to 127.
  • The tape's timing: CHEW 80 delays a note's start by about +2.4 ms on average, with a spread of 0.59 ms between notes (+1.2 to +3.2 ms over twelve notes), and the end of a note by +3.0 ms ± 1.6.
  • Dropouts: none measured on the held A2 at CHEW 80 (no dip of 6 dB or more; the deepest was 5 dB over 2.1 s). A separate 12-second hold counted dips of 6 dB or more: 0 at CHEW 0, 4 at CHEW 30 and 60 (deepest 6 dB), 8 at CHEW 100 (deepest 11 dB) and 15 at CHEW 127 (deepest 20 dB); the 4 dips at CHEW 60 also appeared with DROPS 0, so they were not isolated as dropouts.
  • Chopped: a 60 ms note is 40 dB down 14 ms after the key goes up and 60 dB down at 18 ms; after the 2.4 s held note it is 60 dB down at 36 ms.
  • Level: matched to the bank reference on the splice phrase (−18.1 dBFS RMS, peak −12.9); phrase (b) reads −17.6 with a peak of −12.5.
  • Costs, honestly: about 2177 host instr/sample worst case (the original: 1384); CHEW accounts for about 770 of it. The device build was not run and the render time on the device is not measured.
  • Tricks: untested on this patch: the SLOBBER slop ride, SEQ held (Tape Stop), the kill switch (HEEL), GROWL, ALLEY, DRAIN, ENV>O2. OSC 2 LEVEL 0 still modulates through X-MOD (measured on this patch's held A2: the render with X-MOD 100 differs from X-MOD 0 by 3.1 dB re the signal); how that sounds is untested.

card.sound: An anxious, thick drone that bites, like touching a live wire. A stack of pulse waves in the high register, with an upper layer an octave and a fifth above, run through a resonant filter that zaps at the start of every note. It is fat and bright, medium-to-high, and it never sits still: the voices wander on their own and the whole stack leans and jitters in pitch. It is dry and each note is chopped off the moment you let go.
card.gear:
• Korg Mono/Poly (in unison) — the stack: fat, drifting.
  • Minimoog — thick.
  • Korg MS-20 — the bite: the bite.
  • Roland Jupiter-4 — fat, wobble.
  • Sequential Prophet-5 (early revisions) — the unsteadiness: drift.

Closest to: a Mono/Poly in unison with MS-20 bite.
card.play:
• Register: high. It was voiced on a held A4 (3.5 s), eight 110 ms bites (E5, A4, C5, D5) and a held A3, plus the pilot phrases; low notes and other registers are untested.
  • It is a UNISON of 6 voices on one note, so legato does not re-fire the envelopes: a key held while the next goes down slides to it and the zap does not happen again. Play it detached for the bite. Chords play one note (the last).
  • Chopped: a bite is 40 dB down 18 ms after the key goes up, and a held note is 60 dB down at 26 ms. No echo, no spring.
  • The drift, measured by the engine's own log over the held A4: the six voices sit at static offsets from -9.3 to +7.2 cents from each other's centre and each wanders by 3.8 to 5.7 cents (s.d.), over ranges of up to about -22 to +26 cents; on top of that a smooth-random pitch LFO leans the stack by up to 19 cents at about 0.28 Hz (a new target about every 3.6 s), each voice at a different point of it. The audio alone cannot show this: the stack's own beating moves its measured pitch by more than the wander does. The SLOBBER slop ride is untested on this patch; its recorded effect is to multiply a patch's own slop, about 3.0 times at VINTAGE 127 (voicing README, section 5).
  • The zap, stated honestly: the measured top-end burst (energy above 1.2 kHz in the first 40 ms against the body) is -2.0 dB on the held A4 and +0.5 dB on a bite: the bright body (centroid 3855 Hz on the wire phrase, 71 % of its energy above 1.2 kHz) reduces the measured burst. The darker version rendered alongside measured +4.6 dB. This one was approved by ear, as rendered; the burst number is a diagnostic here, not a promise of a big zap.
  • Level and attack: matched to the bank reference on the wire phrase (-17.9 dBFS RMS, peak -8.9; phrase (b) reads -18.2). The original sat 4 dB over the reference with a peak of -2.2 dBFS at VOLUME 100. Struck from silence on a high probe note, the stack rises from 10 to 90 % of its plateau in about 11 ms; with one or two voices the same patch reads 1.2 to 1.5 ms, which suggests the six voices beating, not the envelope.
  • Costs, honestly: about 1298 host instr/sample in the worst case (the original: 1985, with its effects); no GROWL. The device build was not run.
  • Tricks: untested on this patch: SEQ held (Tape Stop), the kill switch (HEEL), GROWL, any effect. The echo and spring are off; the original's echo and spring were removed. Turning DRAIN up is untested.

card.sound: A tight, plucky square stab with a resonant plop on the front, drenched in spring. The note has a body now and it holds for as long as you play it; the spring rings on after the note and is the sound of the patch. It is a wet, springy, boingy reggae stab.
card.gear:
• Korg MS-20 — the resonant filter plop: plucky, biting.
  • Roland SH-101 — the tight, quick stab: tight, punchy.
  • Moog Prodigy — the single raw square: fat, cheap, raw.
  • Fender spring reverb tank (Twin Reverb style) — the drench: springy, boingy.
  • Roland RE-201 Space Echo — the dub-style tail: warm.

Closest to: an MS-20 plop into a Fender spring tank.
card.play:
• Register and gate: off-beat two-note stabs of about a tenth of a second, around A3 to C4 (the skank it was voiced on). Other registers are untested.
  • The plop is still there, softer. The resonant filter sweep is still audible by tone (measured: the first 23 ms of a stab are twice as bright as the next 67), but the first 20 ms is now only about 3.5 dB louder than the body, so the pop is softer than in the first version of this patch.
  • The body survives the gate. The filter now rests above the played notes instead of closing under them, and the amp holds (measured: the level falls under 4 dB inside the gate; the first version fell almost 17 dB and left a hum).
  • The spring is the sound: it ships at DRAIN 90. Measured, the spring's return is about 6 dB under the dry note over the stabs (6.1 dB), and by time window after a stab it is about 22 dB under the note in the first 20 ms, about 6 dB under in 20 to 100 ms, and about 6 dB louder than the note in 100 to 250 ms, which is natural for a spring: it is what rings after the note stops. The tail takes about 1.1 s to fall 60 dB. The gap between stabs sits about 16 dB under the stab (measured -16.3 dB on variant E, the committed one; ../09-skeenhead.md, round-2 table).

card.sound: A bright, struck chime built from a square wave with a second oscillator that zings down in pitch at the strike. The ring decays slowly, over a couple of seconds, and a gentle slow shimmer in pitch and level fades in after the strike and sways the ring. A small slap echo and a touch of spring sit behind it, and everything passes through a narrow, honky mid-band like a small horn speaker. There is no tape in it.
card.gear:
• Yamaha DX7 (tubular-bells voice) — FM clang, inharmonic. OSC 2 sits +15 semitones above OSC 1 (a ratio of 2.38) with X-MOD 25. Through the filter that partial reads −34 dB under the note at C#6 and −18 dB at C#5 (measured, first 100 ms); the strongest partial after the note is the square's third harmonic at −15 dB (C#6). So it is faint at the top of the keybed. "Clang" is not measured.
  • A music box, struck — fast-decay, nostalgic. Not carried: the ring takes 1896 ms to fall 40 dB at C#6 (measured), a long ring, not a fast decay. "Nostalgic" is Vincent's word and is not measured.
  • Finger cymbals (zills) — bright metallic ping. The centroid over the first 20 ms is 2096 Hz at C#6 and 1958 Hz at C#5 (measured). "Metallic" is not measured.
  • A transistor radio or van horn speaker — band-limited, honky, lo-fi. The filter read with white noise peaks at 1099 Hz, with a −3 dB width of 898–1345 Hz; 0.4 % of its energy is under 400 Hz and 4.1 % above 4 kHz (measured). On the chime melody through the whole patch: 0.0 % under 400 Hz, 0.45 % above 4 kHz, centroid 1262 Hz. "Lo-fi" is not measured.

Closest to: a music-box chime played through a cheap van horn speaker.

The reference for the register was Vincent's two phone recordings of a real ice-cream van: the chimes sit in a narrow band centred about C#6 (about 1110 Hz), notes about 580 ms apart. Those measurements of the recordings were rough (speaker, street and engine are in them), and the van chime's own spectrum is not known, so the partials above were measured on this patch, not copied from the recordings. Nothing here says the patch matches the gear or the van: it was built toward the descriptions, by measurement, and approved by ear (with the tape on).

Provenance, built by ear: the patch was built by ear on the OberVave engine from field recordings Vincent made of a real South African ice-cream van parked outside his house (two phone recordings, Nov 2026). The register (chimes centred about C#6), the note spacing (about 580 ms) and the short bright strike came from those recordings; the measurements of them were rough. Nothing is sampled, and no audio from the recordings is in the firmware or the repo.

Vincent's ear, after hearing the final (11 Nov 2026), not measured: he hears it as closer to an arcade or vintage video-game chime than to finger cymbals ("a cleaner ring"). The bank had nothing in that register before this patch.
card.play:
• Register: voiced for A4 to A6. RMS over the first 300 ms of one struck note, with the centroid over the first 100 ms: A4 −22.1 dB / 1950 Hz, C#6 −18.5 dB / 2183 Hz, A6 −20.1 dB / 2563 Hz (measured). A4 sits 3.6 dB under C#6 and A6 1.6 dB under it; neither end falls away in that range. Nothing outside A4–A6 was measured.
  • Ring and overlap: the ring of a C#6 falls 6 / 12 / 20 / 40 dB in 252 / 550 / 1030 / 1896 ms (the whole patch; 276 / 584 / 938 / 1943 ms at C#5; the voice alone reads 1954 ms to −40 dB at C#6). With notes 580 ms apart several rings overlap. POLY 5 is set; POLY 4, 5 and 6 against POLY 8 change the level of what rings by at worst −0.1, −0.6 and −0.7 dB on the melody, −0.2 to −0.3 dB on the fast run's tail and 0.0 dB on the chord, so no cut ring is measurable (random oscillator start phases make a sample-for-sample comparison useless; not isolated whether stolen voices were the oldest).

  • Fast run: eight 120 ms notes 160 ms apart (C6 up to G6 and back) read −16.6 dB RMS with a peak of −9.9 dBFS, no clip.
  • Shimmer: a TRI LFO (the stock preset it was voiced from uses a sine, which this engine does not have): 0.8 Hz, pitch ±9.4 cents by the law, amp 40, delay 40, PHASE SYNC so every note starts it the same way. On a one-voice sustained probe the pitch wobble reads 5.1 cents s.d. (−8.2 to +8.3 cents, strongest component 0.80 Hz) and the level swings 2.8 dB; this is the LFO alone, as there is no tape. "Dreamy" and "ethereal" are Vincent's words and are not measured.

card.sound: A dry, punchy unison bass: every voice stacked on a single note, fat and thick, loosened just enough that the stack breathes without ever going seasick. It is warm with a driven edge that stops short of fuzz, and each note is chopped hard on release: no spring, no echo, no tail, only the silence after the hit. This is the flagship, the DØG-5 signature, and it has presence: it sits forward and fills the room.
card.gear:
• Minimoog in unison — the stacked saws and the octave-down body: fat, sub-heavy, thick.
  • Moog Taurus bass pedals — the weight at the bottom: deep, floor-shaking.
  • Roland SH-101 — the quick attack and the hard stop: tight, punchy.
  • Oberheim OB-Xa in unison — the wide, full stack with its warmth: fat, full, warm.
  • Korg MS-20 — the grit in the filter when it is pushed: nasty, biting.

Closest to: a Minimoog in unison with Taurus weight.
card.play:
• Register: low. Roots and octaves from about A1 to A2 are the sweet spot, and it is built for single-note bass lines and chopped roots. The very bottom (A0, and the A1 below it) is partly under what small speakers and many PAs reproduce: most of the audible weight is in the 60–150 Hz band and above, and the sub-octave saw underneath is inaudible at the very bottom. On a full-range system you feel it; on a laptop you hear the body, not the floor.
  • Touch and gate: staccato to medium. Eighth-note chops (roughly 130 ms notes) are its home: a hard body, a stop, and the impact comes from the silence after. It also holds, as a wall of low unison, with a slow slight beat that stays under control.
  • One note at a time: it is a unison. All eight voices play the one note you are holding, so chords are not available; use it for lines and roots.
  • Tricks that suit it:
  • ALGORITHM slop ride (SLOBBER): loosens the stack further, from controlled to loose. Untested on this patch; the patch's own slop is mild, so there is room.
  • Tape Stop (SEQ held) as an ending: the whole low stack dives. Untested on this patch.
  • Kill switch (HEEL) for a dead stop; the patch has no tail to hide behind.
  • Filter DRIVE (the MIXER page, knob 4): the gentler route to more grit. It is already part of the sound; pushing it adds harmonics without squashing the dynamics.
  • GROWL (adding it live): the Psych Chain macros are 0 on purpose. GROWL only starts to do something above about 28 and compresses past about 40, so it is a big step, not a touch; it also costs noticeably more CPU than the filter drive.
  • ALLEY, DRAIN, CHEW: at 0 on purpose (dry and punchy is the sound); untested on this patch, and a wash will blur the chop.
  • Level: it deliberately sits about 1.5 dB above the bank's usual level, for presence. Expect it to jump out a little when you switch to it.

card.sound: The aggressive chord stab: a fifth built into every note, a hard filter pluck, and a short slap-back echo right behind it. Each note is a detuned pair, so it is fat and punchy rather than thin, warm rather than icy, with a bright snap on the front that settles into a solid body. It is dry apart from the slap: no spring, no long wash, just the stab and its quick echo.
card.gear:
• Sequential Prophet-5 — the stab itself, with weight behind it: punchy, fat, warm.
  • Roland Juno-60 — the short, snappy pluck: plucky, punchy.
  • Roland Jupiter-8 — the open top on the attack: bright, full.
  • Korg MS-20 — the bite when you dig in: biting.
  • Roland RE-201 Space Echo — for the short delay: slap, warm.

Closest to: a Prophet-5 stab through a Space Echo.
card.play:
• Register: low to low-mid. Single notes and fifth-based riffs (roots and octaves around A1 to A2) are its home ground: every note already carries its own fifth, so one finger plays a power chord.
  • Touch and gate: short and hard. A stab of roughly 150–200 ms is the target: bright snap, a body that rings a moment, then the slap. The patch has no gate-length control; how long the stab is comes from how long you hold the key.
  • Chords, honestly: because the fifth is built into every voice, a chord made of fifths stacks fifths on fifths and turns into a sus2-style cluster (root and fifth together sound like root, fifth, ninth). That is the engine doing what the patch asks, not a fault. Play single notes and fifth-based riffs; use real chords sparingly.
  • Polyphony: every note is two voices (the DUAL pair), so a chord is three notes at most by design: three notes use six voices, a fourth still fits (all eight voices), and a fifth steals from the notes before it.
  • CPU: it is heavier than the single-voice version, which is the price of the fatter pair. Check the GLOBAL page's render time if you stack it with other heavy settings.
  • Tricks that suit it:
  • The slap (ALLEY): it is already on, and it is what makes this the Space-Echo stab. Turning it up for a longer echo, or tapping a time in on the BBD page, suits it. Untested on this patch.
  • ALGORITHM slop ride (SLOBBER): loosens the pair. Untested on this patch; the patch's own slop is mild.
  • Kill switch (HEEL) for a dead stop: it clears the echo as well, so nothing rings on. Untested on this patch.
  • Tape Stop (SEQ held) as an ending. Untested on this patch.
  • GROWL / DRAIN / CHEW: at 0 on purpose (the patch's drive is the filter DRIVE, already in the sound). A spring will blur the stab; untested here.

card.sound: A plain voice made of two saw waves played through a low-pass filter with a short envelope, dry, with chords and single notes both playable. Nothing is added to it: no modulation, no echo, no spring, no tape and no drive.
card.gear:
• Sequential Prophet-5 — a plain saw, the filter open. Not carried. The filter is not open: it is a 24 dB low-pass at CUTOFF 80 with RESO 20, and there are two saws, not one.
  • Minimoog — one raw oscillator. Not carried: OSC 2 is on (a saw, LEVEL 100, 4.7 cents from OSC 1).
  • Roland SH-101 — a saw, the filter open. Not carried for the same two reasons.

What was measured: through the filter, the harmonics of C3 are −7.9 / −14.3 / −18.0 dB for the 2nd / 3rd / 4th (a plain saw is −6.0 / −9.5 / −12.0), and the 10th harmonic sits 6.8 dB under the 1/n law at C3 and 15.8 dB under it at C5. So B is two detuned saws through a closed-ish filter, not a plain saw. The strike centroid is 620 Hz at C3 and 1618 Hz at C5.

Closest to: an analog two-saw init patch. "Raw" and "blank" are Vincent's words and are not measured. Nothing here says the patch matches the instruments above: it carries none of them literally.
card.play:
• What it is: the engine's own default program, with one change, VOLUME 97 (the default is 100). It is not the single raw saw with an open filter and flat envelopes that the brief described: POLY 5, two saws 4.7 cents apart (OSC 2 FINE 70), a 24 dB low-pass at CUTOFF 80 with RESO 20 and KEY TRK 64, the filter envelope (ENV AMT 90, attack 20, decay 70, sustain 40, release 60), the amp envelope (attack 10, decay 70, sustain 100, release 60), VINTAGE 30, SPREAD 60, every effect at 0. Slots 33–99 hold the same defaults as INIT, with VOLUME 100.
  • Chords: POLY 5 plays chords. Levels over the note-on region: −18.05 dBFS on the stabs phrase, −22.9 dB on the low chopped riff, −17.7 dB on the held chord (A2 E3 A3); the peak is −5.6 dBFS over every phrase tried. K-weighted level on the stabs −18.5 dB.
